In Exhibit 490, those civilian and municipal authorities rejected the decision of Colonel Blaskic to replace Stjepan Tuka, thereby continuing a process during which the issue of whether an order would be carried out or not was resolved some weeks later, a process that involved not only the military quote, unquote, chain of command, but civilian, religious, cultural entities. That was what I wanted to say for the record. Thank you for hearing us out, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, for the record, as you said it, you are saying that. Please conceive, I'm not taking sides, conceive there might be another approach. You cannot prevent a civilian community, I'm speaking in general terms, you can't prevent civilian population and its representatives from feeling moved by a decision. If tomorrow, for example, an authority in France or the United States or Egypt or any other country were to take a decision which does not please the population, you cannot prevent the authorities from saying that the decision does not appear just to them, or it appears illegal to them, you cannot prevent that, that is not the question. We are discussing whether the accused, yes or no, had the duty, the obligation to consult with the civilian authorities. We have recorded your comments. Now I would like us to go on. Mr. Nobilo, I'll give you the floor; but if you're going to take up the same arguments, I'm going to interrupt you immediately. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It's a different argument, Mr. President. These documents show that the decision of Commander Blaskic on going to war and on dismissal was not carried out. That's all. And they prove that if he doesn't consult the municipal authorities he cannot carry them out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's your thesis, and the Judges have noted it, as they will note the thesis of the Prosecutor. This is the last document, and we have noted it is not complete. What is the question that you, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Preliminarily, Mr. President, I think this is complete, and we will gladly bring up the original and show it to the Court. Nevertheless, we will move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a document that comes from the Central Bosnian Operative Zone command dated 7 May 1993 at 15.00 hours, and the subject is the announcement to the commander of the Busovaca Nikola Subic-Zrinski Brigade to the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the Fojnica Nikola Subic-Zrinski Brigade. "On 6 May 1993 we received announcement number 7-01-170/93, from the legally non-existent HVO command of Fojnica municipality. The self-proclaimed commander, Stjepan Tuka, stating that, quote, that the Fojnica municipality HVO command has made the decision that the current command of the 3rd Battalion is to continue to activities in the same composition and with Commander Stjepan Tuka as its head with regard to the above mentioned announcements. 1. The institution of the HVO command of municipalities does not exist within the legal system of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. Municipal Croatian Defence Councils were set up as municipal civilian authorities with a statutory decision of the municipal executive authority and the municipal administration." Citing the official Gazettes of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, number 91. "The foundations of the armed forces were laid, and its structure and system of command and control were determined by a decree on the armed forces of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna," again official Gazette number 692, "and the regulations issued in compliance with this decree. "Based on the above mentioned regulations, the Nikola Subic-Zrinski Brigade is active in the area of the Busovaca Fojnica municipalities when something is unclear. From the above mentioned it can be concluded that the civilian and military authorities are precisely delineated, and the institution of the HVO command of the municipality is both formally and legally contrary to the fundamental regulations of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, i.e. it is not legal, and neither are the decisions it makes. "Pursuant to Article 34 of the decree of the armed forces of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, Mr. Stjepan Tuka is relieved of his position as commander of the 3rd Battalion of the Nikola Subic-Zrinski Brigade, and a new person has been appointed to perform the duties of commander. "The decision of the so-called HVO command Fojnica municipality for Stjepan Tuka to continue performing the duties of commander of the 3rd Battalion -- next page Mr. Usher, next page -- "Mr. Tuka is to continue performing the duties of commander of the 3rd Battalion is a serious violation of the unified system of command and the obligations to implement decisions, orders and instructions of the superior command. "Such activities are particularly serious in the circumstances of the struggle of the Croatian people for its existence and identity in historic areas. Actions and activities of the so-called command and the self-proclaimed commander give grounds for disciplinary action to be taken and criminal charges to be filed with a competent military Prosecutor, which will be done." Now, Brigadier, are you familiar with the initials in the lower left-hand corner, NS, as the drafter of this document? Or is it not on your copy?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not see the initials on my copy. But I know the initials SV, SHV, those are the initials of the typist, Mrs. Stefica Vinac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know about the issuance of this document by Commander Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't know about the issuance of this document, and I don't know that it was issued by Colonel Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, in this document, this document that came from the command of the Central Bosnian Operative Zone, states quite clearly that the HVO command of the Fojnica municipality is legally non-existent; isn't that correct? And I direct your attention to the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: The HVO command, as far as I understand the structure as it was at the time, it refers to the command of the civilian authorities, because reference was to the command of the battalion, and the battalion commander. This is rather ambiguous when it says HVO command, because you have seen from the documents when a commander is being dismissed, it is the battalion commander that is being dismissed and not the HVO commander. So, the terms are ambiguous. So, my conclusion would be that this applies to the civilian authorities, that is what can be inferred from the context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, let me direct your attention to paragraph 1. Blaskic quite clearly draws a distinction between the municipal civil authorities and the structure and system set up for the armed forces; does he not? Take a quick read at that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I have looked at the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there is a separation, Blaskic discusses a clear separation of powers between the civilian authorities and the armed forces, or the HVO; doesn't he? He cites to the two locations in the Narodni Lists or the Official Gazettes that support his position; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I cannot answer this question. But if I can say, the commander of the Operative Zone, General Blaskic, knew exactly the difference between the competencies of the civilian and military authorities. But he was aware of the situation, and that is why we had such instances. This is the first time that he tried to replace a commander without consultations, and we see the kind of problems he came up against. That is what I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The question was much simpler than that, Brigadier. It was a very simple question. It was simply to -- I thought you agreed about paragraph one, that Colonel Blaskic had made the distinction between the military and civilian systems. I don't think we have to go any further than that. Of course if you don't want to answer, you don't have to. Continue Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I know that General Blaskic knew the difference between the civilian and military chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Continue, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, in the next paragraph Blaskic says that the HVO command of the municipality is not legal, and neither are its decisions. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by that, sir, he completely rejects the authority of this body to issue any legally binding decisions on him as the commander of the HVO; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Please. It says clearly here that in the legal structure of the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna, and if this is General Blaskic's text, then, in saying this, he wanted to make it clear that he would be the one who would decide on the appointment of commanders. And according to the regulations, that is how it was envisaged, and that is how I read this sentence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the next paragraph he calls upon his authorities, in Article 34 of the Official Gazette that we talked about this morning, which gives him the authority to appoint and dismiss. Do you see that in the first line in number 2?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he relieves Stjepan Tuka of his command.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: General Blaskic gave the order for the replacement, in line with the regulations that you have referred to and the authority that he had. He issued that order, and he refers to those provisions in that text, that he was entitled to do that. The General claims that he has the right to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to Article 34 of the Narodni Lists, he does have the legal authority to dismiss Stjepan Tuka; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and that is on the basis of what he wrote the order on his dismissal. But it was not carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As we move on to paragraph two, he notes that any challenge to that authority is a serious violation of the unified system of command; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: General Blaskic was aware of that, and that is why he issued orders, based on his formal authority. But I explained what happened on the ground; General Blaskic knew that there wasn't a unified system of command, and that military rules were not being respected; that is why we had so many orders and appointments that we have reviewed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me clarify this question. Does Blaskic say in this document that any challenge to his authority under Article 34 is a challenge to the unified system of command? Does he say that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: We can see from the text what the General says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Any challenge, Brigadier, to that authority, would have been a challenge to his authority prior to the dismissal of Tuka, or in the appointment or dismissal of any commanders at any time; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is so. Any failure to carry out the General's orders is in direct contradiction with the authority that he formally had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he asserts his authority under Article 34 to appoint and dismiss, categorically, as he sees fit; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document speaks for itself. We could go over every sentence, but what's the point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would think that you're right, but we have to recognise that sometimes your witness goes as far as he can in contesting some of the sentences. I would like also to say to Mr. Kehoe that it is self-evident, so let's go on, move faster.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The bottom line, Brigadier, is contrary to the wishes of the municipal authorities in Fojnica, Stjepan Tuka was dismissed; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is not correct. Let me explain. Stjepan Tuka was replaced after General Blaskic requested assistance from the top level leadership of Herceg-Bosna, the political leadership of Herceg-Bosna. I don't know exactly whom he addressed, was it President Boban, to exert their influence on the municipal authorities, and only then was the decision carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But we're trying here to find the truth, that's what it is about. Was he dismissed or was he not? It's a clear question. Was he or was he not dismissed? According to this document, was he or was he not dismissed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: It was a compound question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm asking the witness the question, Mr. Hayman. I have the right to ask the question. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe's question was compound. I'm not objecting to your question, but the earlier question was compound, it had two components.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe's questions, apparently, to me it seemed whether or not Tuka was dismissed. He said first I don't agree, and then he spoke about commander authority. So, I turn to the witness and ask whether or not he was dismissed, or did he keep his command. You are answering me now.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, the commander of the Fojnica Battalion, Mr. Stjepan Tuka, was dismissed after the commander had issued his order and ensured support of the political authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I understood it, it's been recorded. All right, he was dismissed. I would like to say to you, Mr. Hayman, that you do see that when you very frequently refer to Rule 68, you see that a document can, when you refer to Rule 68, which is your right, let me point out to you that in support of the document, a document can be read as exculpatory in several ways. A document can go contrary to a witness statement and in favour of the accused, and that same document can go contrary to the accused in favour of a thesis supported by the witness. Therefore, I think it's more complicated than that. The document is a perfect example of what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I agree with the Court but the wording of Rule 68 requires that if a document is capable of interpretation favourable to the Defence, it must be disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, doesn't that language imply a right on the part of the Prosecutor to make precisely that judgement? Shouldn't the Court take the position that, provided the Prosecutor does not act unreasonably, the Prosecutor is entitled, within certain reasonable limits, to make exactly that judgement, as to whether the document is capable of supporting the case for the Defence. Now, the Prosecution takes the view, so I understand the position, that these documents are not reasonably capable of supporting the case for the Defence. What the documents show is that the municipality, the civilian authorities, mounted what I would call a political opposition to the implementation of General Blaskic's order. Civilian authorities did not take the position that General Blaskic was not competent in law to issue such an order without prior legal, prior consultation with the municipal civilian authorities. I don't see that in the documents. I don't see that the municipal authorities were taking this position, that, look, you cannot issue an order of this kind without prior consultation with us. If they had taken that position, then I, for one, would have been prepared to understand and empathise more fully with the position which you are taking.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If I may, just very briefly, Your Honour, because I think this is a fruitful question. The position of the Defence, and I think the testimony of the witness has been, there was a legal framework for appointing commanders, but there were extra legal pressures and processes, which were in fact more important than the legal framework. These documents, in the view of the Defence, demonstrate the functioning and coming to bear of pressures through these extra legal channels and processes. To address the question of Rule 68, Your Honour, Rule 68, I submit, imposes an objective standard as to whether something is exculpatory or not. Of course, the Prosecutor makes the, must make some initial determination himself, but ultimately it is an objective standard. It is not a decision that can be delegated, permanently delegated by the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I would just like to stress what the President mentioned before, that in any democratic society, and like the one in Bosnia and Croatia and the one in the United States, there are organisations, there are NGOs who can express their opinion. I don't think that the President of the United States is not, it does not mean that the President is not entitled to take a decision if all the NGOs express their opinions. Organisations can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think that is absolutely right, and it is an indication in some ways of a healthy quasi-democratic debate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Not legally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: What is important here, Your Honours, Mr. Tuka was not replaced during the time period these discussions, consultations, infighting were going on. He was not replaced. Our client's order was not carried out for a period of weeks. And that, I think, is very, very important. That's what we're saying. And perhaps my colleague has something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You are right, but these things were decided. The conclusion was that these organisations do not have any binding authority. Whether it took time or not, the result was clear, apparently.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But they had the power, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: To speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Not only to speak, Your Honour. Commander Tuka was not replaced during this time period of these dialogues and processes. They had the power to block the order of our client of 20 April 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Let's say there was a dialogue.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: But they held the cards, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: For the time being we're talking about dismissal of Mr. Tuka, and we may later argue as to the results. Perhaps during the time there was a replacement there was another phase, and the accused was aware there was pressure being brought to bear. I don't know that, you have to show it. I think for the time being we will stay with this point, the Judges have expressed their point of view. I simply wanted to say to you, Mr. Hayman, that application for Rule 68 can, for one same document, support the accused, but not necessarily the witness statements. Or vice versa. We usually take our break when people begin to get excited. I think, then, lunch will calm everybody down. We will resume at 2.30 --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.00 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please resume and have the accused brought in. (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, ready to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's true, you can't proceed without the witness, you're right. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours and Counsel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Brigadier.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, during your testimony on direct examination, you gave us some information about orders that were issued by various Commanders. Before I talk to you a little bit about those orders, I would just like to ask you about the training that officers receive, such as yourself, for reserve officer training, what type of training did you receive in the JNA on the writing of orders and what are orders supposed to contain?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am prepared to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. President, Your Honours, the training of officers, reserve officers, of which we have spoken here before, while they are in training in the reserve officers' school, as I mentioned, they were trained to be able to command to the units at the level of platoon or company. In the school, while I went through the training, I was writing, in other words, I was trained to write orders at a level of squad and platoon. This was done in this school and this is what everybody who was in the school was trained to do. As far as the JNA is concerned, I cannot say exactly what was taught in military academy during those four years with respect to writing orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, basically, one of the things that should not be in the order is some language that you discussed in, I believe it was Defence Exhibit 293, if the assistance of the witness, if the witness could take a look at that. 293 is an order from Mr. Cerkez, I believe. If I am not mistaken. And the -- is that 293? Mr. President, I am just waiting for the witness to get the document so he can take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, you noted, and I think you were referring to the first page, the second paragraph, "Last night Muslim forces constantly conducted re-grouping in order to realise their sinister plans." And Mr. Nobilo asked you a question, the question was on page 12.372, and the question was: "We have a specific style of writing here, for instance, reference to Muslim forces sinister aims. Is this an example of the type of reporting you refer to in the morning?" Your answer, Brigadier, is "yes." Excuse me, "Yes, a part of the text in this report is an eloquent example of the kinds of reports I was referring to because commanders or members of Brigade commands, due to lack of military training would write this kind of combat order using terms which are not important for military terminology." Do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall, but I have a combat report here and you have just mentioned combat order and there is a major difference between the two, so it may be an interpretation thing, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am just reading what you said and I think the words counsel was focusing on were the words "sinister plans" and your opinion that they were not proper in either a military order or a military report?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. This vocabulary would never have been used by officers who have a certain level of education and training in writing documents to their superiors. But in the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, such as it was, these terms were encountered quite frequently because the warring sides in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in all three sides, were using very inappropriate terms. Let's recall that after Washington and Dayton, the International Community took a position and said that the Serbian army has to be called the army of the Republika Srpska. That the Bosnian army had to be called the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Croatian army had to be called the Croatian Defence Council, so that was a very widespread usage.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let me turn your attention to Kiseljak and what was going on in Kiseljak in the 16th or April of 1993 prior to the outbreak of hostilities on the 16th and 17th of April. Isn't it true that the ethnic tensions between the Muslims and the Croats in Kiseljak was very high?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is correct. Because the conflict in the Kiseljak municipality between HVO and the BH army started as early as January of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, by the time a conflict broke out on the 16th of April, it's fair to say, is it not, Brigadier, that the tensions between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims in Kiseljak were very high?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that, that this was the case, and the reason for it is that after the conflict of January, 1993, some certain commissions were established and those commissions were given the task to lower the tension and carry out the tasks, which I think we have seen here, and we saw that both the representatives of both the HVO and the BH army were members of those commissions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, I mean, were the tensions high or low in April 16th? Were the emotions running very high or very low in Kiseljak on the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: In order to fully respond to what happened on 16 April in Kiseljak, I would like to request to be given the report from Kiseljak from that date in order to fully recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't have that, Brigadier. All I am asking is you just based on what you said before, that tensions between Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats in Kiseljak were very high in April of 1993. That's all. Prior to the outbreak of the conflict. I don't have a particular report.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: In my personal view, and this is my personal conclusion on the basis of my entire insight of the Central Bosnia territory, I believe that the tensions were running high and I believe that when we sent the report on the 16th about what was going on in Vitez and Busovaca, that we were attacked and that this, I believe that this information did contribute to the situation in Kiseljak, because we, that is the Operative Zone command, issued orders to lower tensions in order to avoid an open conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, prior to the outbreak of hostilities on the 16th of April, Blaskic made frequent trips to Kiseljak, travelling in a BRITBAT warrior, an armed personnel carrier, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that or I cannot deny that either because, again, let me ask you, did he go five times or ten times? As far as I know, he did not go there frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, based on the documents submitted by the Defence, and we can pull those out, he was certainly in Kiseljak the weekend before hostilities broke out in Vitez. I mean that the document that the Defence put in says he was there from the 9th to the 12th of April in Kiseljak, and I think you said in your testimony that he often went to Kiseljak because his family was there.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, General Blaskic would frequently go to Kiseljak before the conflict in January, before the road at Kacuni was not cut off at the length of 11 kilometres. And after the cease fire was signed --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you ask the witness to speak a little more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Brigadier, I think the translation booth, I don't mean to interrupt you, sir, the translation booth just asked you to slow down a bit, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I understood. Mr. President, let me repeat everything I have said. Before the conflict in January 1993, General Blaskic did go frequently to Brestovsko, his hometown, and Kiseljak because this was possible. After the conflict in January, 1993, after the road between Busovaca and Kiseljak had been cut off, that is placed under control of the BH army at the village of Kacuni, when General Blaskic wanted to go to Kiseljak, he would have to write to UNPROFOR and ask to be driven to Kiseljak, which was only accepted if he was going to attend certain meetings organised by UNPROFOR and UNPROFOR work representatives would be present there until he came back. He had to always state why he was going where and how long he was going to stay there. This is what I know about these activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact of the matter is that after the road was cut off in mid-January, he made frequent requests of BRITBAT and he made frequent trips to Kiseljak to visit his troops and visit his family? That's all I am asking you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: He did not go to Kiseljak frequently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. We'll come back to that because we'll show you some documents, but at this point you would agree based on the Defence documents, he was in Kiseljak the weekend before the hostilities broke out if Vitez; correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, my learned colleague is misleading the witness. We would like to see the document, which the document that he is referring to, which put Blaskic in Kiseljak on those days, and this is implicit in the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Prosecutor did not say that, Mr. Nobilo. The Prosecutor asked a series of clarifying questions about the visits to Kiseljak. The witness and the Prosecution do not agree and they are in agreement with adverbs like "frequently" or "not very often." I think the Prosecutor said what he had to say properly and at the proper time he will show the document. There is nothing unusual about that. He is not taking the witness down any wrong path. The Prosecutor simply noted the witness' answer. Continue, please, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, with the ethnic tensions being high in Kiseljak, Blaskic knew that those ethnic tensions were high in Kiseljak as well as you knew that, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Regarding tensions in Kiseljak, I gave you my personal view. My personal view is that the tensions were high not only in Kiseljak, but in all other places. What General Blaskic's opinion was, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me show you Defence Exhibit 299 to start with. Mr. Dubuisson, if we can pull 300 as well, Defence Exhibit 300, both of those documents, it would be helpful. Exhibit 299 is the preparatory order to the Ban Jelacic Brigade that was introduced by the Defence that you recognise, that you identified. Isn't that correct, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document drafted in the command of the Operative Zone, signed by General Blaskic, and it is a preparatory combat order for the tying up of a part of the Muslim forces that are attacking the HVO. That is exactly how the document is titled.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In No. 1, the second to last sentence, the sentence that reads: "In the combats that raged yesterday." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The sentence reads: "In the combats that raged yesterday, the enemy used the favourite method of the Chetniks, pushing women and children in front to use them as a shield and then to occupy the main strategic objects." If we move down to 4: "Keep in mind that the lives of the Croats in the region of Lasva depend on your mission. This region could become a tomb for all of us if you show lack of resolution." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn our attention to the Defence Exhibit 300. An order dated 17 April, 1993, which you not only recognise, but you wrote. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The order for combat operations, dated 17 April, 1993, at 23.45, that orders combat operations to begin the following morning at 05.30. In No. 1, under "Enemy," Blaskic, or you, wrote: "The enemy continues to massacre Croats in Zenica where Muslim forces are using tanks to fire at people, mostly women and children." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do. May I provide an explanation for this statement?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 17th of April, in the territory of Vitez and Busovaca displaced persons were already arriving from Zenica. They were carrying with them this kind of rumour. In order to check, because we couldn't go to Zenica, I know that the Commander contacted UNPROFOR and asked them if he could go and see what was happening in Zenica. So, the wording of this text reflects what I have just said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let me show you another document, sir. Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 494, 494A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, unfortunately there is no French version as yet of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let me turn your attention to the document. Do you recognise Colonel Blaskic's signature?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, this is a document signed by General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: With his stamp?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, this is the stamp of the Operative Zone command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is again a document -- excuse me, this is again a document that is written to the Ban Jelacic Brigade in Kiseljak, dated 19 April, 1993. Time: 18.45. Let us turn to point 5 in this document. You're welcome, of course, to read the entire matter, but the questions that I am interested in will be focused on No. 5: "The future of all Croats of Busovaca, Travnik, Vitez and Novi Travnik depends on your success, whereas in Zenica -- some words are illegible -- in any concentration camp, in particular, Gornji Zenica, where our people who fled from the centre of Zenica are being slaughtered even today. There is a massacre." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go one last document, 456/50, which is another order being sent to the Ban Jelacic Brigade, approximately two hours later on the 19th. Hour: 21.40. 456/50. Do you have that, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I have the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is a document, as I just noted, of 19 April, 1993. Again, to the Ban Jelacic Brigade at 21.40 hours by the packet system, I think you will agree with me. And let's read No. 3: "At the moment, the Croatian people of Zenica are going through a most critical period. They are literally being slaughtered." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I see it, and the explanation why it is worded in this way is as follows: I said that after the 16th, 17th, 18th and 19th, displaced persons were coming from Zenica, bringing with them such rumours and reports, and so the Commander in view of the complexity of the situation we found yourselves in, let me remind you that on the 19th, were the strongest attacks on Vitez and Busovaca and according to reports coming from Kiseljak, he would issue this kind of order.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you were asked about this terminology by Mr. Nobilo during your direct examination, and I am referring counsel to page 12.407, and you were asked about why Blaskic used this methodology to send the Ban Jelacic Brigade into combat. Line 13: "Why did General Blaskic need to order the Ban Jelacic Brigade into action in such a dramatic way? Such an emotional way? Why didn't he just order, go ahead, do such and such a thing? Why wouldn't that have been militarily more proper?" Your answer was: "Yes, that's correct. It would have been more proper in military terms. However, as I mentioned there were very, very few militarily educated officers with proper military training and enough experience." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do recall that, and I still think along the same lines as I said then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when this was going to the Ban Jelacic Brigade, Mijo Bozic was the commander of the Ban Jelicic Brigade; wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Mijo Bozic was the commander of the Ban Jelacic Brigade. But if I may add, because of the lack of military organisation and lack of understanding of the seriousness of the situation on the part of certain commanders, and the difficulties encountered by neighbouring units in Busovaca, Kiseljak and Vitez, we had to use this kind of language for people to realise how serious the situation was because reports coming from Busovaca and Vitez spoke of the seriousness of the situation, and that can also be seen if we look at the model in relief, we see the position of the town of Vitez and Busovaca, as of the 17th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't you tell us both in direct and cross-examination that Mijo Bozic was a graduate of the military academy, just like the accused, Colonel Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Mijo did graduate from the military academy; but while he was in Kiseljak he would not recognise, from an order using the regular language, how serious the situation was. The commander would have never used these words if it wasn't so serious. Because the 19th of April was a day which was decisive for us, to be or not to be, to defend Busovaca or to lose it. So, this is the text of a man pleading out of despair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, the fact of the matter is that Mijo Bozic was a trained officer that went to the military academy and the JNA, and he understood orders to do things; didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, but I think the witness has answered that question, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We will move on, Judge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These orders were sent to the Kiseljak Ban Jelicic Brigade at a point when ethnic tensions in Kiseljak were very high; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: These orders were not sent to Kiseljak because of ethnic tensions. These orders that went to Kiseljak were sent there for Kiseljak to engage forces of the BH army that were attacking Busovaca. They were not sent there to heighten tensions, under no circumstances; because the war was already on, it was a state of war. So, there is no point in saying whether there was heightened ethnic tensions or not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when Blaskic writes to the Ban Jelacic Brigade, Brigadier, and tells them that Croats are continuing to be massacred in Zenica and being slaughtered in Zenica on the 19th, that was done to inflame the passions of the Ban Jelacic Brigade; wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it was not. The aim of these orders was to engage the forces of the BH army. This reference to massacres and slaughtering, I said what my sources were. Perhaps General Blaskic had some other even more specific information. But I know that we asked UNPROFOR to go to Zenica and check whether this was indeed happening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they went to up by Kuber, based on one of your orders about a slaughter in Jelinak, and they found nothing; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. We had a report that this was happening at Kuber, as well, and we asked UNPROFOR to go there. UNPROFOR officers went there, examined the situation, and we knew that it was not true. But, if you get a report like that in a situation of war, you must not, you don't have any time to speculate whether it is true or not. If you have no other information, that is the information for you, until it is proven false.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, isn't it true that Blaskic, as a trained soldier, knew that writing these kinds of orders about slaughters taking place in Zenica, that it was clearly foreseeable that it would inflame the passions of the HVO soldiers in Kiseljak? Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what General Blaskic had in mind at the time. But I know that the aim of these orders was to engage the enemy forces and to ease the pressure on Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on, Brigadier. I just want to clarify a couple of things, if we could just check one thing that you said. You noted the numbering system on these documents, and you noted that the numbering system on the documents, some discrepancies in that regard were illustrative of the lack of HVO organisational structure; do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said -- I apologise, microphone?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sometimes you lean on that and it hits the buttons down.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, when defining the reference numbers used in the HVO, if we look at this particular document dated the 19th of April, at the time we did not receive any standard instructions as to how this should be done. We received such instructions towards the end of 1993. This kind of numbering was the numbering that we introduced in the Operative Zone command, and it is the system that we used; whereas each of the brigades had their own system of numbering documents. For example, the number 406, or rather 01, that means that it is a commander's document; number 4 indicated the month; number 406, that is the number under which it was registered in the file, and in the records where record was kept of all incoming and outgoing documents. That is how the numbering was done, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't the formatting of that numbering system following what had been set out in the Narodni Lists for formatting these numbers?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: In this case, and in this period that we're talking about in April 1993, that was not so. I cannot remember now, but we had some documents here when we received instructions from the main headquarters as to how we should proceed. Then those instructions were followed, both in the Operative Zone command and all the subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you a document, sir, from the Narodni List. Take a look at this, and I would ask you if this was the format that was followed in the Central Bosnian Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 495, 495A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Take a look at these articles, Brigadier. I ask to you take a look at specifically articles 2 and 3. In those articles, doesn't that article 1 indicate a numbering system; for instance, 01 for documents of the HVO, and then reference numbers are discussed down in article 3? Isn't that the formatting structure that Colonel Blaskic adapted for use within the HVO Central Bosnia headquarters?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me repeat my question. The numbering system that was set forth in articles 2 and 3; isn't that the basic numbering system that Colonel Blaskic adapted for use in the Central Bosnian Operative Zone? I show you article 2.1, with the documents of the HVO being 01, and the use of a reference number and slashes after the figures in the year. Isn't that the system?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. In April in 1993, until we received regulations regarding the formatting of the numbers from the Ministry of Defence, we used the method of marking that we saw in the previous documents, and we introduced that method internally within the Operative Zone. From article 2 of the Official Gazette, we can see that the reference numbers refer to ministries or departments in the Croatian community of Herceg-Bosna. This applied to the internal organisation of the government of Herceg-Bosna. So, on the basis of this Narodni List, the Ministry of Defence elaborated its own procedure and defined the system of numbering at lower levels, and we received those instructions towards the end of 1993. When we received that document, which was based on this one, we began marking documents accordingly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you would agree with me that in the lower right-hand corner, or I'm not sure that's true in your original, that this article setting out the numbering system was enacted in Mostar on the 14th of October 1992; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that can be seen from this document. But the defence department, for its organisational entities, of which we were one as the Operative Zone, elaborated its principles at the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We don't need to belabour this point, the document speaks for itself. Thank you, Brigadier. Let's move on to a series of orders that were introduced by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With your assistance, Mr. Dubuisson, if I could have Exhibit 263, 267, 268, 269 and 270.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, please continue, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I'm just waiting for these documents to be given to the Brigadier, in any event.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we're talking first, Brigadier, about Defence Exhibit 263 and the number is 01-4-190/93; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask you, Brigadier, with the President's permission, could you take the marker to your right and just write that number on the easel that is to your left? If could you do it big enough so the camera can pick it up, sometimes when we write small it's difficult to see. If you could put your -- all I'm saying, if you could write it large enough so the cameras can pick it up. So use your best judgement on that. If you would just write that number 01-4.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Complies).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I ask you one more time if you could just probably double the size of that so they can pick it up, so they can pick it up on the cameras? It's a little difficult to see it that far away.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Complies).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can take a seat, sir. Thank you. Now, Brigadier, tell me a little bit about this numbering system that was employed in the Central Bosnian Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Is it 01 or 07, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's 01.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: To me it looks like 07, because I am -- we haven't put the right document on the ELMO, or what? Oh, I see, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think the document on the ELMO is wrong. I think the original is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, I apologise. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, I think you told us before that the 01 is an order that comes from Colonel Blaskic, the number 4 is the month, the number 190 is the number in sequence, and the year is 93; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that was the system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me about the rest of the system. After this has been signed by Colonel Blaskic or someone on his behalf and it's given a number, how was it logged into the records?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I will describe it as I remember, though I didn't keep the logbook. As far as I recall, there was a book, a logbook, into which all documents were entered. Those that were being sent from the Operative Zone command to superiors, and to subordinates, commands, orders, reports, the entire correspondence. Also, a record was kept of everything received, orders from superiors, other reports and information. As far as I remember, that was how it functioned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, if we go through these documents and we move through 267, 268, 269, and I'd like you to review those before you focus on Exhibit 270; could you do that for me, please?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the numbers of the documents so I know I have the right ones in my hands?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, we just discussed 263, and we then go to 267, 268, 269 and then 270.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have looked at these documents that you have mentioned, the three documents, and I said that during the direct examination by Mr. Nobilo that I noticed that these documents do not bear a number, this reference number is missing. That is the difference between this document and document number 263.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I want to focus your attention, before I go on to the other documents, I would like to focus your attention on Exhibit 270; and that does have a number, doesn't it? That should be the information.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the number there, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: The document is number D270, it has been entered in the logbook under the registration number 240.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Could you write that number on the board underneath the one that you have just written? If you could take the marker again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, if we could just help him a moment with that. Just write the number.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Complies).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, stay there, Brigadier. You would agree with me, based on the content of that document, that the 8 is a typographical error and should be a 4; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, this is an error, and there are a number of such documents. But if you look at the time when this document was written, it is the morning when the attack occurred on the territory of Vitez municipality, it is probably due to haste and panic. I've even seen some documents where there is an error regarding the year, though it is obvious from the text that it refers to another year. So, this is a mistake.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have no doubt what you're saying. I just ask if you could correct that, knowing that the date is a 4, could you put down the 4 over the number 8 so we know that is in fact an order that was issued in April, as opposed to in August?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Complies).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could stay there Brigadier. At approximately what time was the 240 order on the 4th, approximately what time was that issued? I guess it was sometime after 5.45 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: This order, as far as I can remember, it's not an order, actually, it's information. There's a difference. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about when the document was issued. Approximately what time do you think it was issued?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I recall, it could have been about 9.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, could you throw down your best estimate of 09.00 under that number as the time?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Complies).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if I could just turn your attention back to, with the assistance of the usher, Exhibit 263. And if you could put the time down for the order that we have on the 14th of April 1993, and if you could put that time down, time and date, if you could.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Complies). I need to indicate the year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sure, you could just throw the year in, and the time, which I believe is 9.30 -- excuse me, 10.30. Sorry, I can't even read the numbers. 10.30. One last thing, and the date on the bottom number, which is 16-4-93. The one, the second number, I believe you told us was on the 16th, is that right? I'm talking about 1-4-240, that was issued on the morning of the 16th. Can you just write down --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Excuse me, what am I supposed to write down?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just write down the date, so we know what date that number was issued.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: (Complies).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. You can have a seat. Now, Brigadier, based on that, would you agree with me that between 10.30 in the morning on the 14th of April 1993, and approximately 9.00 in the morning on the 16th of April of 1993, we had approximately 50 documents either incoming or outgoing, coming out of the headquarters -- or outgoing, excuse me, because the incoming would have their own numbers.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: The exact number can be found by subtracting the top number from the bottom number and you said it was how many?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My math is not the best and take 190 from 240, come up with 50.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, 50.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we have 50 outgoing documents that have numbers on them during that time frame; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Sent and received, Mr. Kehoe. You said sent and received, I am not sure I understood that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are numbers that are outgoing, issued, outgoing. The incoming had their own numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, I needed that clarification. Thank you very much. Do you agree with that, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not agree with that, Mr. President. When I said, as far as I recall, that is the way the correspondence was registered or logged, the incoming mail, I believe that it was the same logbook that both the incoming and the outgoing documents were logged. So there would be a logistics, personnel, information, public information, anything that was drafted and anything that was incoming, I think was locked in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I am just asking a general question. Are you sure about that? This is the first time that I see an important civilian military echelon. That would be only that kind of numbering system because it would be hard to find one's way around. All right, let's go on. It just seems a little strange to me, that the same numbers be used. Mustn’t be very easy for Colonel Blaskic, all of a sudden when he wants document number such and such and someone brings him a document that was received and not one that was sent. That wouldn't have made things very easy. But, all right, that's not a problem for right now. I was just a bit surprised, but I asked for the clarification because the Prosecution had spoken about incoming and/or, so I want to be sure here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, to follow up on the President's questions, Brigadier, none of the documents that were presented by the Defence, or had been shown to you, have a number given to it that is incoming, isn't that so? All of the numbers that were given to documents executed in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, were outgoing documents; isn't that accurate?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said what I remember, which is that the same logbook was used to enter whatever was drafted in the command and whatever was incoming. I am trying to recall how it worked. This was an improvised system, Mr. President. It is a system which we instituted without any particular standards, and the staff that worked on this did not have any experience in these activities and I know how the procedure went. So if a document would come in, let's say it was received through the packet system, the officer would look at it and then it would initial it or something and mark it, and then it would be sent to a person who would log it. This document would be then entered and given the next number. Let's say we've reached number 300, let's say we receive a document which was just drafted and signed by the Commander and then this person would just enter it as the next number, 301. This is how I remember things being done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, of the documents that are before you, Exhibits 263, 267, 268, 269 or 270, are any of these your documents?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let me review them in order. Document No. 263 was drafted by me, and I signed it, and I was authorised to do so by the Commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, maybe my question wasn't clear. Did they belong to you? Did you have them in your possession prior to coming here to testify? Any of these documents that we talked about.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: These documents were shown to me by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. So you did not have them in your possession before you came here?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I only reviewed the documents which were shown to me by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Brigadier, in a system -- just following up on the President's questions -- in order to have an contract record keeping system, it's important to have the documents numbered, such as the numbering that's on Exhibit 263; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. There has to be one, but this is what we have before us is what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, take a look at Exhibits 267, 268 and 269. That is the order from the 15th of April at 10.00, the order of the 15th of April at 1545 and the order of the 16th of April at 01.30.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I reviewed the documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, none of those documents have numbers on them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, and I pointed it out when asked by Mr. Nobilo. I asked him why these documents were not properly numbered, the gentleman from the Defence should be asked this question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, as a military man, it's important to have numbers on these documents in order to follow the sequence of those documents; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is important too. But even more important is what this document refers to and how it is going to be implemented. But if we did not have this numbering system, our work would have been completely disrupted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Brigadier, you noted during your direct examination that when you saw these documents in the headquarters of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, they did have numbers on them.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said, and as I recall, it would have been illogical for such documents not to have numbers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take a look at Exhibit 268. And I ask the witness to be shown the French translation as well as the English translation, as well as the original Bosnian or BCS versions. Do you have all of those before you, Brigadier?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have the Croatian version. I cannot read French. I believe this could be French.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I hope English as well. But I sympathise with your efforts because I can't read BCS. Now, Brigadier, on the document that you have before you, 268, it appears that the number has been removed, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot say that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, turn to the French and English versions, the other two translations of this document. It would appear that those were copied and the numbers were removed on those as well; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot give you a specific answer to your question. I can only guess. I see the document in Croatian. It is clear that there is no number on it, and I find it illogical that it should not have a number because I do know this document. I drafted this document. I put this mark on it, so I do recall both the contents and form of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate what you're saying, Brigadier. But I ask you to take a look at the French and the English versions in the place where the number should be and it would appear, does it not, that the number has been removed from those two documents during copying, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: It does not seem to me to be that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have an extra copy of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, in order to cut short this debate, we stipulate that there were numbers here, but they were removed. But Brigadier Marin has no knowledge whatsoever about it. So, we stipulate that, there is no need to pursue this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, if that's the case, then maybe we should talk about this outside the presence of the Brigadier because this is a matter that we should discuss. That's the position, with the Court's permission, the Prosecutor would like to discuss this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We will have a closed session right after the break. Take a twenty minute break and everybody can think about this very significant and interesting question. I suggest that after twenty after four we resume in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (The witness entered court).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Brigadier, you're back with us after this brief closed hearing, and I give the floor again to Mr. Kehoe to continue with his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. With the assistance of the office of the registrar, can I have several documents, and if I could read them in sequence to be shown to the Brigadier. They are, should I read them off? D211, D334, D359, D361 through 366, D376, and D384.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If the witness could be given all those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As soon as I see a document, I begin to look to the left to see if there is a number there, or see what the number is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As regards the document on the easel, do you want it to have a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be 497.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do we have a copy of it for us? We have it as a Defence Exhibit, Mr. Dubuisson.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, it's a Prosecutor's Exhibit. It's the one on the easel, the numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's 497, that is the document that's on the easel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Does the Brigadier have all those documents? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, he was given everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. I would also ask that these documents be handed out, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be 498/1 and then according to your numbering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brigadier, let me ask you a question: Do you know Major General Primorac?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I do know Major General -- I do know Major General Ivica Primorac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is he, sir?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do know Major General Ivica Primorac, and as far as I know, he works in the defence ministry in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me take a look at the documents that have been admitted into evidence during the course of your testimony, Brigadier. If we can compare them to the orange folder that you have in your hands, and the first particular insert is a receipt from Major General Primorac, and I want to direct your attention to tab 2. I would like you to compare that with Defence Exhibit 211. Mr. Usher --

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO MARIN (Resumed)
utterances.text: My apologies. I did not have interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment. I would like to understand your question better, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, the question is going through these documents, and the documents are in tabs 2 through 11. They are the documents that were provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by Mr. Primorac. The Defence has introduced those documents, as I have reflected, in the front page, D211, D234, et cetera, and a reflection of those documents will indicate that on each one of the documents provided by Major General Primorac, there are no numbers, whereas the numbers that were in the Defence documents, there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to see them on the screen. Can we see them on the screen, please? The interpreters will have problems also if they don't see them on the screen. If you have problems, Mr. Kehoe, I will try to find my document 211, but it has to be on the ELMO. All right, 211. All right. I have found the Defence document under number D211 and D211A for the French version. Now you want us to make a comparison of this with the documents that were tendered from the Prosecutor's Office or the Defence? I am lost here. Could you explain it to me, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, Ivica Primorac provided these documents to the Prosecutor and the Defence provided them with registration numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's exactly my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, I am delighted. For once we're getting answers even before the questions are asked. That's really wonderful. What conclusion are you trying to draw from this? That is, drawing from your comment. Mr. Nobilo is saying he has a document which was submitted with a reference number. I think it's a small "g" next to the 17 March 1993; is that right, Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is -- actually, that is not the reference number. If we put the B/C/S number on the ELMO, you can see on the Defence copy that there is a number above the 12th or the 17th of March, 1993 -- 17th of March. The English translation does not have that number, but the original B/C/S does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: What is your conclusion, or, in fact, what is your question? But for the time being, this is discussion going on between the Defence and the Prosecution. I am not sure what is it you want to ask the witness, I don't know what he is going to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question of the witness is that with all of these documents that he admitted, these documents that we listed that had numbers on them, the documents that we have in Exhibit 498 are exactly the same, or virtually exactly the same except for the numbers being deleted, and the ones being deleted were the documents that were provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by Brigadier General Primorac -- or Major General Primorac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: If the witness is going to be forced to review and compare these 10 or 15 documents, we might as well recess for the evening, Mr. President. But what's the point of asking the witness to undertake such a review? It's apparent on the face of the documents that we were able to get documents with the reference numbers and we've provided them in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The point is this, Mr. President, and it's quite clear, that the Office of the Prosecutor has been attempting to get documents from the Bosnian Croat side of the federation pursuant to binding orders since January of 1997, and the point is that we haven't gotten documents in their total unredacted form and what we have gotten are documents such as these, and the point is that the Office of the Prosecutor wants compliance with all of those documents and doesn't want this type of response coming from the office -- from the federation side or the HVO side of the federation. Now, the next portion of this is the series of orders that were handed down by the defence department for officers, such as the Brigadier, to gather documents that were in compliance with the binding order issued by this Court and provide them to the HVO by a certain date. Now, that's another series of documents. The question on that score is: Has the Brigadier actually been given that order; and if, in fact, he and anybody else in the HVO turned those documents over to an archive, who, in turn, has not turned those documents over to the Court? Now, this is a particular individual who is a high-ranking office in the HVO in the one unit, or one Brigade -- not Brigade, but one large part of the army left, who should know full well whether the HVO should be complying with this Court's order. That's where were going in this regard. Given the fact that this Brigadier is here, these questions need to be answered in order for us to ensure whether or not compliance is ever going to come, whether or not he got this order, whether or not no one told him about it. There are a series of questions that must be asked of this officer in order to find out what exactly is going on and why this Court's binding order has not been complied with. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. President, that's beyond the scope of the direct examination. We don't object to a straight question to the witness: Has he had any responsibilities or obligations with respect to responding to any orders of this Court for documents? But let's get to the point, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First of all, you've noted that the Defence does not object your asking these questions of Brigadier. Second comment is, now the Judge speaking, I would like to know if you're contesting the substance and authenticity of the order? I think that's important. And with respect for binding orders, you know what the opinion of the Tribunal is on this; that is, the unfortunate order to obey orders from the Tribunal. Before I break for session, I would like you to ask your question clearly. It will be the only question that you're going to ask and then we will resume tomorrow morning at 9.45. Don't lose sight of the essential point, that is, we have an order from Colonel Blaskic that was dated 17 March, 1993, and which has a reference number in the Croatian version with its reference number and I can see that in March they use the numbers of the official journal contrary, perhaps, to what he had said a bit hastily before. But ask your question, and then tomorrow you may, if you like, contest the substance of the order. Try to get to the essential point; otherwise, we're going to be here for a long time this evening and for a long time after that. This is the last question then. That is the last question that the interpreters can interpret today. Ask the witness the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we're dealing with, in fact, 11 orders. The 11 orders that the witness has in tabs 2 through 11 of the Defence has admitted with orders that we have received -- excuse me, the Defence has admitted with numbers and we have received from Major General Primorac without numbers and this witness has identified them, and I would like to ask him whether or not he sees that they don't have numbers and that, at the time he saw those numbers in Central Bosnia, they did, when he saw those orders, they did, in fact, have numbers. That's the essence of this particular exhibit, that these numbers have been removed as well, at least the ones that have been given to us by Major General Primorac. Now, I don't think that can be done in one question. I invite the witness to examine this document overnight and we can answer it in one question in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: So stipulated, Mr. President. Obviously the numbers have been removed. You can look at the two documents. You can compare the documents. Obviously the numbers were removed before they were given to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Either the Defence are saying that the numbers were removed, I suppose for the same reasons that you mentioned a while back; is that right, Mr. Hayman? This is a public hearing, so we're not going to go into the details, but the same reasons?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We were not privy to the production of these records. This was a secret proceeding of which we were not involved. We don't know exactly under what terms they got these redacted documents or what they were told. All we can say is what's the point of asking the witness to compare --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But these were directly provided to you; is that right? They were provided to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Presented, apparently all the same documents with registration numbers. The Court has those now. But what apparently Mr. Kehoe wants to ask the witness is, one at a time, to compare them and ask him: Does the number appear on one document and not the other? We submit that's silly. That's a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It begs the question as to why the number is removed from all the documents that are given by the Prosecutor and the Defence seems to have numbers on all of these documents. That's a significant question for this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: The question is, what is the question for the witness? We have a witness here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Exactly, who just identified every one of these documents as documents that he saw in Central Bosnia with numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: There you are. It sounds like the question has been answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Let me turn to the witness. Brigadier Marin, when you were in office with the accused, first of all, did you see the documents, and when you saw them, if you did, did they have the numbers that are in the version which has been provided by the Prosecutor? That is for D211, provided by the Defence without the number and for the document which is in the 498 --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. The Defence provided all the documents with registration numbers and the Prosecution provided them without the numbers and they're now making an issue out of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Exactly. Because the ones we got were pursuant to a binding order coming from this Court to the Bosnian Croat side of the federation who gave us these documents without numbers. And the question remains: Why? Now the person who has identified these documents in this courtroom as having been executed in 1993 is seated in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Brigadier, what's the answer to the question that the Prosecutor asked you? I am not going to dare ask it again. I am not sure I really understood it. But you heard what he asked you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, before arriving to testify here, I saw the documents produced by the Defence, that is, the documents with registration numbers or reference numbers. Before coming in this courtroom, I never saw the documents which were provided by the Prosecution. When these documents were being produced in 1993, I confirmed that I recalled the contents of these documents from 1993. Before I came to this courtroom, I saw these documents offered by the Defence. These documents, which were offered by the Prosecution, I did not see before coming into the courtroom, and I see now that they are without this registration number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We consider that the witness has answered. I think we're going to suspend the hearing, and we will see one another again tomorrow at 9.45 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
